newsitem.title: UK: Segers claimed earnings came from stolen cars.
newsitem.headline: Segers claimed earnings came from stolen cars.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers told police he had been stealing luxury cars because he didn't want them to know he had been forecasting the results of soccer matches, his lawyer said on Monday.

Segers is on trial accused of accepting bribes to rig matches in England's Premier soccer league. He denies the charge and says only that he received money from a Malaysian businessman to provide forecasts for Dutch soccer matches.
He told the court he only learned that forecasting matches was against English Football Association rules a few days before he was arrested.
He made up the story about stealing and selling cars to explain away the large sums of money he paid regularly into a Swiss bank account, his lawyer Desmond Da Silva said.
"To play in England was a dream come true for me. To put that in jeopardy..." Segers told the court on his first day in the witness box.
He is standing trial along with former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim.

They are accused of being part of a lucrative Asian gambling ring. Telephone records compiled by the prosecution show that the four were in frequent telephone contact, expecially on the days of big soccer matches.

Segers told the court he had never thrown a soccer game and that the season during which police alleged he threw matches was highly successful for his club Wimbledon. Segers, 35, was asked by his lawyer whether he had ever thrown a game of football in his life. "Never," he replied.
"Nobody asked me to throw a game, I've never thrown a game."
Segers explained his frequent telephone conversations with Fashanu by saying that both were having extramarital affairs and were arranging to cover for each other if their wives called.
"I played a few away matches," said Segers, referring to his own affairs. "I asked John quite a lot to cover for me."

Segers, who declined to have a lawyer present during police interviews, said that most of his income outside football came from a business, Ties International, which he owned jointly with a Dutch friend.

The company, which made club ties for several soccer teams, made around 90,000 pounds ($150,000) profit in one year alone. Segers said he was given most of his share of the earnings in cash which he paid into his Swiss account.
But because he did not want to reveal that he had been evading taxes he told police that the money in the Swiss account had been transferred from Jersey, another tax haven.
"Is the tax man interested in your affairs?" Da Silva asked him.
"I think so," said Segers, smiling and pointing to a man at the back of the court. "I think that is Mr Taxman there."

Da Silva told the court that Wimbledon had lost or drawn 14 matches in a row in the 1995/96 season while Segers was recovering from a knee operation. When Segers returned in late December, the team started winnning again.
"That was a nice Christmas present," said Segers.
